title: Right to left
hook: Hebrew is read from right to left

segments.voice: Yesterday, the alef-bet: all consonants, and the reader brings the vowels. Your line was twenty-two letters. How many names could you say? Today, which way those letters run. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-eight.

Hand a Hebrew prayer book to someone who has never held one, and watch their hands. They open it the usual way, cover on the left, and find themselves at the last page. They flip, frown, flip again. Then someone leans over, smiling, and turns the whole book around. The spine goes on the right. The first page is where an English book would end. And on that first page, the first line starts at the right-hand margin and runs toward the left. Nothing is backward. It's just facing the other way. Today's word is the direction.
screen: `OPENED FROM THE WRONG END.` → `THE SPINE ON THE RIGHT.` → `THE LINE STARTS AT THE RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Right to left. Turn it four ways. First, the line. Hebrew is written and read from right to left. The pen starts at the right margin and travels left, and the eye follows it. Second, the book. Because each line runs leftward, the whole book follows: the binding sits on the right, and pages turn from left to right. A Hebrew book begins where an English one ends. Third, one word, slowly. Take the opening of the line that, by tradition, is said morning and night, from Deuteronomy: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." In Hebrew, the first word is Shema. Three letters. On the far right, shin, the letter from two days ago, with its three arms. To its left, mem. And to the left of that, ayin. Shin, mem, ayin: right, middle, left. Shema. Read the other way, it falls apart. Fourth, why it matters for someone just starting. A reader whose hands and eyes were trained left to right has to slow down here. The eye wants to jump the wrong way. That slowness isn't a problem to fix. It's a doorway. You can't skim a language you have to read against your habits. Every word asks for a little attention, and attention in prayer is something the rabbis prize: they call it kavanah. So for now, let the eye start on the right, and let it take its time.
screen: `THE LINE RUNS LEFTWARD.` · `THE BOOK OPENS FROM THE RIGHT.` · `SHIN, MEM, AYIN: SHEMA.` · `SLOW EYES, CLOSE ATTENTION.` · then, large: `RIGHT TO LEFT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trace one word. Settle, and breathe. Hold out your open palm, or rest your finger on the table. Start at the right. Draw shin: three small arms rising from a base. Move left. Draw mem: a shape like a box, open at the bottom left corner. Move left again. Draw ayin: two short strokes meeting in a long tail that drops below the line. Shin, mem, ayin. Then trace the same path once more, slowly, right to left, and say the word softly as you finish: Shema. If you pray, it's the word that opens the Shema. The bell holds the time.
Right to left. The way Hebrew runs: from the right margin, from the right side of the book, one slow word at a time. Today's word.
Your line: right to left. Today, read one thing slowly, a sign or a sentence, and let it take as long as Hebrew would. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Hebrew is written and read from right to left, so Hebrew books and prayer books open from the right; children learning to read trace words from the right margin, often starting with familiar words like Shema.

original.note: Hebrew: hear. Three letters, read right to left: shin, mem, ayin.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hebrew is written backward.
what it means: it simply runs the other way: each line from the right margin leftward, each book from the right.
what a scholar hears: Shema, the first word of Deuteronomy 6:4, whose three letters a beginner traces right to left: shin, mem, ayin.

notes: Editor pass: cut the muddled 'road built from the other side of the river' image from the hook; 'the line Jews say morning and night' softened to 'the line that, by tradition, is said morning and night' (no claim about all Jews).
Deuteronomy 6:4 quoted as JPS 1917; confirm exact wording and punctuation.
'The line Jews say morning and night' rests on Deuteronomy 6:7 ('when thou liest down, and when thou risest up'), paraphrased; confirm phrasing doesn't overstate practice.
Letter shapes in the practice (mem as a box open at the bottom left, ayin with a tail below the line) are simplified for listening; a Keeper may want to refine.
